extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan), scholars studying natural law and religion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and organizing Hobbes' normative claims about religion, human nature, and natural law from a Leviathan excerpt. Focuses on the seeds and causes of religion, criteria for religious authority, and Hobbes' definitions of right, liberty, and the laws of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion of Ghosts (natural seed of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion that apparitions seen in dreams or visions are real external substances (Ghosts, Imagines, Umbrae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men naturally mistake creatures of the fancy for real spirits because they cannot imagine incorporeal things; this propensity is one of the four natural seeds of religion. Examples and explanation: dreams, looking-glasses, and apparitions make people believe in external spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of second causes (natural seed of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not knowing what we call 'Causing', people infer supernatural causes from observed sequences without perceiving dependence or connexion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From past likenesses they expect future likenesses and ascribe luck or fortune to unrelated things (examples: demanding another Phormio or Scipio). This leads to superstitious inferences (charming, conjuring) and false beliefs about changing things into other things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devotion toward what men fear (natural seed of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worship naturally mirrors the expressions of reverence used toward other humans: gifts, petitions, thanks, bodily submission, considered addresses, sober behaviour, premeditated words, and swearing by invoking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond these human-like acts reason suggests nothing; further ceremonies are adopted under the influence of those thought wiser. This characterizes ordinary worship practices—rituals are expansions of civil reverence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking casual things for prognostiques (natural seed of religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency to take accidental events or rare occurrences as prognostications or omens of future events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes enumerates many divinatory practices (oracle ambiguity, Sibylline leaves, astrology, necromancy, augury, haruspicy, dreams, omens like ravens' croaking, palmistry, monstrous births, eclipses, comets, lotteries). Shows how easily creditable men can be persuaded by those with skill to exploit fear and ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as product of two cultivators (humane vs divine polity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious customs are cultivated either by men inventing them (humane politiques) or by God's command (divine politiques).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both aim to make people more apt to obedience, laws, peace, charity, and civil society. The former serves earthly rulers and public order; the latter contains precepts for subjects in God's kingdom. Distinguishing origin affects how religion is evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founders' devices to secure obedience and legitimize precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders and legislators often claim divine origin or higher nature to make their religious precepts accepted, and prescribe ceremonies and penalties to enforce obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Numa claiming Egeria's dictation, founders claiming divine progeny, Mahomet's conferences with the Holy Ghost. They also make civil prohibitions appear displeasing to gods, prescribe sacrifices and festivals, and attribute misfortune to anger of gods to maintain order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images, consecration, and endowed revenues to enforce religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing images in picture and sculpture, consecrating lands/caverns/groves/temples, and endowing them with revenues and officers to increase the awe and obedience of the ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes describes this as a calculated means to make people fear and respect gods represented by images and thereby accept the rulers and laws associated with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of natural causes to many gods (fragmentation of agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning specific natural or social functions to many gods (Venus for fertility, Apollo for arts, Mercury for craft, Aeolus for tempests, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multiplication of gods exploits ignorance of causes and produces a variety of religious practices that correspond to different business and passions of men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ambiguous prophecy and divination to manipulate belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Oracles and prophecies are made ambiguous or produced by intoxication/confined conditions to seem prophetic; ambiguous responses can be framed to fit outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes notes intentional ambiguity (and sometimes fraud), the intoxicating vapours at oracles, and later interpolations to ancient prophecies (Sibylline books, Nostradamus) as methods to persuade and control people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoyning belief of impossibilities discredits founders (criterion of wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring belief in contradictions (enjoyning belief of contradictories) shows ignorance and destroys the reputation of a founder's wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes: both parts of a contradiction cannot be true; imposing such beliefs signals ignorance and undermines claims to supernatural revelation (people will not accept revelations that contradict natural reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous conduct of religious leaders undermines sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders who act unjustly, cruelly, profanely, avariciously, or luxuriously betray insincerity and reduce credibility of their religious claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such actions are stumbling blocks (scandals) that make people fall away from the religion because they indicate leaders do not themselves hold the beliefs they promote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private ends (self-interest) discredit religious promoters
rubrics_metrics.description: When required beliefs or practices primarily benefit the promoters (dominion, riches, dignity, secure pleasure), their love and sincerity are suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that if people see leaders profiting, they will attribute the religion to private interest rather than genuine piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony of miracles and prophecy as proof of divine calling
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles, true prophecy (also a miracle), or extraordinary felicity are the testimonies required to prove divine calling and justify additions to religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without supernatural signs, additions to religion obtain only customary belief; miracles function as supernatural signs analogous to natural signs in ordinary matters. Examples include Moses' miracles and prophetic success; the failure of miracles often leads to loss of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of faculties as basis for equality of hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature has made men equal in body and mind such that differences are not significant enough for one to claim exclusive entitlement, yielding equality of hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality explains why two men desiring the same scarce good become enemies and leads into Hobbes' analysis of the state of nature. Illustrative points: weakest can kill strongest by cunning; prudence is experience common to many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal causes of quarrel
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition (for gain), Diffidence (for safety), and Glory (for reputation) are the main passions that make men quarrel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each cause leads to different motivations: competition for resources, diffidence leading to anticipatory aggression, and glory leading to contests over trifles like words or gestures. Useful for diagnosing causes of conflict in a given situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of war in the state of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: War is not only battle but a 'tract of time' in which the will to contend by battle is known; peace is absence of that disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration of time is essential: sporadic fights do not equal war unless there is a standing inclination to fight. This standard helps assess whether a condition counts as war or peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of absence of common power (state of war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a common power to keep all in awe, there is no industry, culture, navigation, building, arts, letters, society; life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hobbes' criterion for the practical value of a common sovereign: the presence or absence of these social goods diagnoses whether a polity provides security and flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing is unjust in a state of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no common power there is no law, and thus notions of right and wrong, justice and injustice, have no place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such condition force and fraud are the 'cardinal virtues'; injustice presupposes prior renunciation or transfer of right. This criterion distinguishes moral/legal evaluations that presuppose society from purely natural acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of Nature (Jus Naturale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty each man hath to use his own power, as he will himself, for the preservation of his own nature (i.e., his life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right is liberty to do or forbear; it explains what individuals may claim by nature before laws. Hobbes uses this as the baseline for later obligations and transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is the absence of external impediments; impediments may reduce power but not prevent using remaining power according to judgement and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes internal faculties from external constraints; useful for evaluating whether someone's action is free in Hobbesian terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Nature (Lex Naturalis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A precept or general rule found out by reason which forbids doing that which is destructive of one's life and prescribes omitting what would destroy it; law determines and binds whereas right consists in liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes Jus (right) from Lex (law): law binds to one course, right is latitude. Law of nature is discovered by reason and forms moral obligations even prior to civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: In the state of nature every man has a right to everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Because there is no common power and all things may help preserve life, every man has right to everything, including another's body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to insecurity; recognition that renouncing or transferring rights is necessary for stable society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Law of Nature: seek peace
rubrics_metrics.description: That every man ought to endeavour peace as far as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot, that he may use all helps and advantages of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First and fundamental law: 'To seek Peace, and follow it.' The second branch is the summary of Right of Nature: defend oneself by all means if peace is unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law of Nature: mutual renunciation of rights for peace
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should be willing, when others are so too, to lay down his right to all things and be contented with as much liberty against others as he would allow others against himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a reciprocity principle (similar to the Golden Rule) and the foundation of covenants: laying down rights is conditional on others doing the same. It explains the basis for forming common power and contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of laying down a right
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay down a man's right is to devest himself of the liberty of hindering another's benefit of that right; it does not create a new right in another but removes impediments to another's use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that transfer/renunciation alters impediments rather than creating new natural rights; relevant to understanding property, covenants, and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renouncing vs transferring rights; obligation and injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: A right is laid aside either by simple renouncing (careless who benefits) or by transferring to a particular person; once abandoned or granted, the actor is obliged not to hinder the beneficiary, and to do so is injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act must be a voluntary and sufficient sign (words, actions, or both). This provides Hobbes' criterion for valid bargains, obligations, and the basis of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs required for renouncing/transferring rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Renunciation or transfer occurs through a declaration or signification by some voluntary and sufficient signs, which may be words only, actions only, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signs determine when a voluntary act creating obligation has occurred; the sufficiency and voluntariness of signs are the criteria for legally binding transfers in Hobbes' account.
